content: Psychological flexibility is the ability to fully contact the present moment and adapt behavior in a way consistent with personal values despite challenging thoughts, feelings, or sensations. It is a central construct in contemporary behavioral health models, notably Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT). Core mechanisms include acceptance (willingness to experience unwanted internal events), cognitive defusion (distancing from unhelpful thoughts), present-moment awareness (mindfulness), self-as-context (observing self), values clarification, and committed action towards goals. Physiologically, psychological flexibility correlates with improved regulation of the stress response and emotional regulation systems. Clinically, higher psychological flexibility is associated with reduced anxiety, depression, and better quality of life across diverse populations. Interventions enhancing psychological flexibility, such as ACT, have demonstrated efficacy in treating mental health disorders, chronic pain, and stress-related conditions. Limitations include variability in individual responsiveness and the need for skilled facilitation. Safety considerations primarily involve monitoring for acute distress during acceptance exercises and ensuring professional guidance. Major synonyms and related concepts include cognitive flexibility, experiential acceptance, and psychological resilience. This module provides robust foundational knowledge, practical guidance, and evidence-based insights for consumers and practitioners interested in the role of psychological flexibility in mental health and well-being.

content: Psychological flexibility refers to the ability to be aware of the present moment and accept thoughts and feelings without unnecessary defense, while still acting in ways consistent with personal values. Psychological flexibility is considered crucial for adaptive functioning and stress management.

content: There are six widely recognized core processes underlying psychological flexibility: 1) Acceptance: willingness to experience unwanted thoughts or feelings without attempting to avoid them; 2) Cognitive Defusion: changing how one interacts with or relates to thoughts, reducing their literal impact; 3) Present-Moment Awareness: mindfulness or conscious focus on the here-and-now; 4) Self-as-Context: observing the self as a consistent perspective separate from thoughts and feelings; 5) Values: clarifying what is personally meaningful; and 6) Committed Action: engaging in behaviors consistent with values. These processes work dynamically to enhance adaptation.
